title: JSX and the Rendering Model
description: What JSX compiles to, render vs commit phases, purity, StrictMode double rendering, and why React re-renders.

blocks.title: JSX and rendering in simple language
blocks.content:
JSX is syntax that describes what the UI should look like. The compiler turns `<Button kind="primary">Save</Button>` into a function call (with the modern JSX transform, `jsx(Button, { kind: 'primary', children: 'Save' })`). The result is a plain JavaScript object called a React element — a lightweight description, not a DOM node.

A component is a function that receives props and returns elements. React calls your component, compares the new element tree with the previous one, and then updates only the DOM that actually changed.

A useful mental model: your component is a recipe, the React element is the printed order, and React DOM is the kitchen that decides what really needs to be cooked again.

Rendering is React calling your component. It does not mean the DOM changes. A component can render many times while the DOM stays the same because the output was identical.
keyPoints: JSX compiles to `jsx()`/`createElement()` calls that produce plain element objects.
Rendering = calling components; committing = applying the minimum DOM changes.
A re-render is triggered by a state update in that component or an ancestor, or a context value change.
Props changing is not the trigger by itself — a parent re-render is.

blocks.title: Render phase, commit phase, and purity
blocks.content:
React works in two phases. In the render phase React calls components and computes the next tree. This work can be paused, discarded, or repeated, especially with concurrent features such as transitions. In the commit phase React mutates the DOM, attaches refs, and then runs layout effects followed by passive effects.

Because render can run more than once, components must be pure during render: same props, state, and context should produce the same JSX, and rendering must not mutate external variables, start requests, or write to storage. Side effects belong in event handlers first, and in effects only when they synchronise with an external system.

In development, `<StrictMode>` deliberately calls components, initialisers, and reducers twice, and mounts → unmounts → remounts effects once. That surfaces impure render logic and missing effect cleanup before it reaches production. It does not happen in production builds.
keyPoints: Render may be interrupted or repeated; commit is synchronous and final.
Impure render code becomes a bug under concurrent rendering, not just a style issue.
StrictMode double invocation is a development-only diagnostic.
Event handlers are the preferred place for side effects caused by user actions.

blocks.title: Pure render vs impure render
blocks.explanation: The bad version gives different output for the same props and mutates its input, so StrictMode and concurrent rendering expose inconsistent counts and surprising parent state. The good version derives everything from its inputs.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What actually causes a React component to re-render?
blocks.answer:
A component re-renders when:

1. Its own state changes through a state setter or `dispatch` (and the new value is not `Object.is`-equal to the old one).
2. Its parent re-renders — by default every child of a re-rendering component renders again, whether or not its props changed.
3. A context it reads with `useContext`/`use` receives a new value.
4. An external store it subscribes to with `useSyncExternalStore` reports a new snapshot.

Changing props alone is not a separate trigger — props only change because the parent rendered. `React.memo` (or the React Compiler) is what lets a child skip a parent-caused render when its props are shallow-equal.
blocks.explanation: A senior answer separates 'render' from 'DOM update' and mentions that parent renders cascade by default, which is why memoisation and state colocation matter.

blocks.title: Does a parent re-render always re-render its children prop?
blocks.question: A `Layout` component holds `const [open, setOpen] = useState(false)` and renders `{children}`. When `open` toggles, do the components passed in as `children` re-render?
blocks.answer: No — not because of that update. The `children` elements were created by Layout's parent, so the element objects are the same references. React bails out of re-rendering an element that is referentially identical to the previous render.
blocks.explanation:
This is the 'lift content up / pass as children' optimisation. Moving expensive subtrees into `children` of a stateful wrapper avoids re-rendering them without any memoisation.

[Further reading](https://react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component#passing-jsx-as-children)
hints: Who created the element objects inside `children`?
Did those objects change identity?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A product page feels janky. The team says 'React re-renders too much' and wants to wrap every component in `memo`. How do you approach it?
blocks.answer:
1. Measure first with the React DevTools Profiler and the Performance panel (React 19.2+ adds React Performance Tracks). Identify which commits are slow and which components dominate them.
2. Separate render cost from commit/DOM cost and from non-React work such as layout thrashing or large images.
3. Look for structural fixes: colocate state closer to where it is used, move slow static subtrees into `children`, split contexts that change often, and avoid creating new object/array props every render for memoised children.
4. Enable the React Compiler where possible — it memoises components and values automatically and removes most manual `memo`/`useMemo`/`useCallback` noise.
5. Use transitions or `useDeferredValue` for expensive updates that do not need to block typing.
6. Virtualise long lists.
7. Re-measure after each change and keep the change only if the numbers improve.
blocks.explanation: Blanket `memo` adds comparison cost and false confidence; most wins come from state structure and from measuring.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Mutating props, state, or module variables during render (e.g. `items.sort()` or pushing to a global array).
blocks.whyItHappens: Code looks harmless in a single synchronous render, and the bug only appears with StrictMode, concurrent rendering, or a second consumer of the same array.
blocks.correctApproach: Treat props and state as immutable. Copy before transforming (`toSorted`, spread), compute derived values during render, and keep side effects in event handlers or effects.

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Keep components predictable: pure render, explicit inputs, and side effects at the edges.
keyPoints: Keep `<StrictMode>` on in development and fix every double-render surprise.
Derive values during render instead of syncing them into extra state.
Use the Profiler before optimising; record the commit duration before and after.
Enable the React Compiler and its ESLint rules to catch purity violations early.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- JSX → element objects; components → functions that return elements.
- Render is calculation, commit is DOM mutation.
- Re-render triggers: own state, parent render, context, external store.
- Render must be pure; StrictMode double-invokes in development to prove it.

Official references

- https://react.dev/learn/describing-the-ui
- https://react.dev/learn/render-and-commit
- https://react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure
- https://react.dev/reference/react/StrictMode

title: Components, Props, and Composition
description: Props as read-only inputs, children and slot patterns, prop drilling, compound components, and ref as a prop in React 19.

blocks.title: Components and props in simple language
blocks.content:
A component is a reusable function that turns inputs (props) into UI. Props are read-only — a child must never modify them. If a value needs to change, the owner of that value keeps it in state and passes down both the value and a callback.

Composition is React's main reuse tool. Instead of inheritance, you build bigger components out of smaller ones and pass UI in through `children` or named props that act as slots (`header`, `footer`, `renderItem`).

Since React 19, function components receive `ref` as a normal prop. `forwardRef` is no longer needed for new code and will be deprecated in a future version.
keyPoints: Props flow down; events flow up through callbacks.
`children` and element props are slots — a flexible alternative to configuration flags.
React 19: `ref` is a regular prop for function components.
Prefer composition over boolean-flag explosions (`isCompact`, `isDense`, `hasIcon` ...).

blocks.title: Compound components and API design
blocks.content:
Compound components share implicit state through context while giving consumers full control over markup: `<Tabs>`, `<Tabs.List>`, `<Tabs.Trigger>`, `<Tabs.Panel>`. This pattern powers most headless UI libraries.

Good component APIs are small, typed, and hard to misuse. Ask: which state does the component own, which state should be controllable by the parent (`value` + `onChange`), and which defaults should be uncontrolled (`defaultValue`)? Supporting both controlled and uncontrolled modes is common for design-system inputs.

Avoid prop drilling deeper than two or three levels for data that many components need; use composition first (pass the already-built element down) and context second.
keyPoints: Compound components = parent provides context, children consume it.
Controlled (`value` + `onChange`) vs uncontrolled (`defaultValue`) is an API decision.
Often composition removes the need for context entirely.
Spread remaining props (`...rest`) onto the root element for accessibility and styling hooks.

blocks.title: Compound Tabs with ref as a prop (React 19)
blocks.explanation: React 19 lets you render `<TabsContext value=...>` directly instead of `.Provider`, read context with `use`, and accept `ref` as an ordinary prop. Consumers control layout while state stays inside Tabs.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What is the difference between props and state?
blocks.answer:
Props are inputs owned by the parent; the child reads them and must not change them. State is memory owned by the component itself; it changes through a setter and triggers a re-render.

The deeper rule is single ownership: every piece of changing data should have exactly one owner. Other components receive it as props. If two siblings need the same data, lift the state to their closest common parent. If a value can be calculated from props or other state, it should not be state at all.
blocks.explanation: Interviewers look for 'single source of truth' and 'derived values are not state', not only the textbook definition.

blocks.title: Resetting a child when a prop changes
blocks.question: A `<ProfileForm userId={id} />` keeps a draft in `useState(initialName)`. When `userId` changes, the old draft stays on screen. What is the simplest correct fix?
blocks.answer: Give the component a key tied to the identity: `<ProfileForm key={userId} userId={userId} />`. A new key makes React unmount the old instance and mount a fresh one, so all state re-initialises.
blocks.explanation:
Syncing state from props with an effect causes an extra render with stale data. The key tells React these are different component instances.

[Further reading](https://react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state#option-2-resetting-state-with-a-key)
hints: How does React decide whether to preserve state between renders?
What happens when a key changes?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: You own a design-system `Button` used in 600 places. Teams keep adding boolean props (`isGhost`, `isIconOnly`, `isLoading`, `isDanger`...). How do you redesign the API?
blocks.answer:
1. Inventory real usage (codemod or AST search) to see which combinations exist.
2. Replace mutually exclusive booleans with a single `variant` union (`'primary' | 'secondary' | 'ghost' | 'danger'`) and a `size` union. Make impossible combinations unrepresentable in TypeScript.
3. Use composition for content: `<Button><Icon name="save" />Save</Button>` instead of `icon` + `iconPosition` flags; add an `asChild`/polymorphic slot only if teams genuinely need links styled as buttons.
4. Accept and forward native props and `ref` so accessibility and form integration keep working.
5. Ship the new API alongside the old one, provide a codemod, add deprecation warnings in development, and track migration with lint rules.
6. Cover variants with visual regression tests and accessibility checks before removing the old props.
blocks.explanation: Strong answers combine API design (unions, composition), migration safety (codemods, deprecation), and verification.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Copying props into state (`const [name, setName] = useState(props.name)`) and expecting it to update when the prop changes.
blocks.whyItHappens: `useState` only uses its argument on the first render, but developers assume it behaves like a binding.
blocks.correctApproach: Read the prop directly, derive the value during render, use a `key` to reset, or make the component fully controlled by the parent.

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Design component APIs for the caller: small, typed, composable, and accessible.
keyPoints: Use discriminated unions for variants; avoid boolean explosions.
Forward `...rest` and `ref` to the underlying element.
Prefer `children`/slots for content over configuration props.
Support controlled and uncontrolled modes consistently in form-like components.
Migrate `forwardRef` components to ref-as-prop gradually; codemods exist.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Props are read-only inputs; state is owned memory.
- One owner per piece of data; lift state to the closest common parent.
- Composition and `children` beat inheritance and flag props.
- React 19: `ref` is a prop, `<Context value>` renders a provider.

Official references

- https://react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component
- https://react.dev/learn/sharing-state-between-components
- https://react.dev/blog/2024/12/05/react-19#ref-as-a-prop

title: State and useState
description: State as a snapshot, batching, functional updates, immutable updates, lazy initialisers, and structuring state.

blocks.title: State as a snapshot
blocks.content:
`useState` gives a component memory between renders. Each render sees its own fixed snapshot of state. Calling `setCount(count + 1)` does not change `count` in the current render — it queues an update and asks React to render again with the new value.

React batches updates from the same event (and since React 18 from timeouts, promises, and native handlers too), so three setters in one click cause one re-render.

When the next value depends on the previous value, use the updater form: `setCount(c => c + 1)`. Updaters are queued and applied in order against the latest pending state.
keyPoints: State values are constant within a render.
Setters schedule a re-render; they do not mutate the variable.
Automatic batching groups updates from the same tick.
Use `setX(prev => next)` when the update depends on the previous value.

blocks.title: Immutability and structuring state
blocks.content:
React compares state with `Object.is`. If you mutate an object and call the setter with the same reference, React may skip the render. Always create a new object or array: spread, `map`, `filter`, `toSorted`, or a helper like Immer.

Good state structure avoids bugs before they happen: group values that always change together, avoid contradictions (`isSending` and `isSent` both true), avoid redundant state that can be derived, avoid duplicating the same entity in two places (store an id, not a copy), and flatten deeply nested data.

Lazy initialisation — `useState(() => expensiveParse(raw))` — runs the initialiser only on the first render.
keyPoints: Never mutate state; replace it.
Derive instead of duplicating (e.g. `selectedItem = items.find(i => i.id === selectedId)`).
Prefer a status union (`'idle' | 'sending' | 'sent'`) over multiple booleans.
Pass a function to `useState` for expensive initial values.

blocks.title: Predict the output
blocks.question: What does the counter show after one click?
blocks.answer: It shows **2**.
blocks.explanation: In this render `count` is 0. The first two calls both queue "replace with 1". The updater then receives the pending value 1 and returns 2. React batches all three and renders once with 2.
hints: What is the value of `count` inside this render?
How are updater functions applied to the queue?

blocks.title: Updating nested state immutably
blocks.explanation: Each update returns a new array and a new object only for the changed item, so memoised rows for unchanged todos can bail out. `remaining` is derived during render instead of being stored.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Why should you use the functional updater form of setState?
blocks.answer:
Because the value you read from the closure is a snapshot from the render in which the handler was created. If several updates are queued, or the handler runs later (timer, promise, subscription), `count + 1` may be based on stale data. `setCount(c => c + 1)` always applies to the latest pending state.

It also lets you keep `useCallback`/effect dependency arrays smaller because the callback no longer needs to read the state variable.
blocks.explanation: Stale closures are one of the most common React interview topics; tie the answer to snapshots.

blocks.title: Mutating then setting the same object
blocks.question: A handler does `user.name = 'Ana'; setUser(user);`. Why might the UI not update?
blocks.answer: Because `user` is the same reference. React compares the new state with `Object.is`; when it is identical React can bail out of re-rendering. Create a new object: `setUser({ ...user, name: 'Ana' })`.
blocks.explanation:
Mutation also breaks memoised children, time-travel tooling, and concurrent rendering, which may observe the mutated object mid-render.

[Further reading](https://react.dev/learn/updating-objects-in-state)
hints: How does React decide that state changed?
Is `user` a new object?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A checkout form has 14 `useState` hooks, several `useEffect`s syncing them, and bugs where 'submitted' and 'error' show together. How do you refactor?
blocks.answer:
1. List every state variable and mark which ones are derivable — remove those and compute them during render.
2. Replace contradictory booleans with a status union: `type Status = 'editing' | 'submitting' | 'success' | 'error'`.
3. Group related fields (form values) into one object or move them to `useReducer` with named actions (`fieldChanged`, `submitStarted`, `submitFailed`).
4. Delete effects that only copy state into other state.
5. If submission is a mutation, consider a React 19 form Action with `useActionState`, which models pending/result state for you.
6. Add tests for each status transition before and after the refactor.
blocks.explanation: Interviewers want to hear 'make impossible states impossible' and 'remove redundant state', not just 'use a library'.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Storing derived data in state and syncing it with `useEffect` (e.g. `fullName` from `first` and `last`).
blocks.whyItHappens: It mirrors how variables work in imperative code, and effects look like a 'watch' feature.
blocks.correctApproach: Compute derived values during render. If the calculation is expensive, memoise it (or let the React Compiler do it). Effects are for external systems.

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Model state minimally and immutably; derive everything else.
keyPoints: Keep state as close as possible to where it is used.
Prefer one status union to multiple booleans.
Normalise entities and store ids for selection.
Use Immer or `useReducer` when nested updates get noisy.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- State is a per-render snapshot.
- Setters queue updates; React batches them.
- Use updater functions for previous-value logic.
- Never mutate; derive instead of duplicating.

Official references

- https://react.dev/reference/react/useState
- https://react.dev/learn/state-as-a-snapshot
- https://react.dev/learn/queueing-a-series-of-state-updates
- https://react.dev/learn/choosing-the-state-structure

title: Lists, Keys, and Reconciliation
description: How keys drive identity, why index keys break state, preserving vs resetting state, and the reconciliation heuristics.

blocks.title: Keys in simple language
blocks.content:
When React renders a list, it needs to match each item in the new list with an item in the old list. The `key` is that identity. With stable keys React can move, insert, or remove items while keeping each item's state and DOM nodes attached to the right data.

Keys must be stable, unique among siblings, and derived from the data — usually a database id. They are not passed to the component as a prop.

Using the array index is acceptable only for static lists that never reorder, filter, or insert in the middle.
keyPoints: Key = identity across renders, not just a warning silencer.
Unique among siblings, stable over time, derived from data.
Never generate keys with `Math.random()` or `crypto.randomUUID()` during render.
Index keys break state when items are inserted, removed, or reordered.

blocks.title: Reconciliation heuristics
blocks.content:
React's diffing is O(n) thanks to two assumptions:

1. Elements of different types produce different trees. Changing `<div>` to `<section>`, or `ComponentA` to `ComponentB`, at the same position unmounts the old subtree and mounts a new one — state is lost.
2. Keys identify children across renders.

State is tied to a position in the tree (plus key), not to the component variable. Rendering the same component type in the same position preserves state; changing the type or key resets it. Defining a component inside another component creates a new type every render, which resets its state every time.
keyPoints: Same type + same position + same key → state preserved.
Different type or key → unmount and remount.
Never declare components inside other components.
You can use a changing key deliberately to reset a subtree.

blocks.title: Index keys losing input state
blocks.explanation: Uncontrolled inputs keep DOM state. With index keys that state follows the position, not the item, so deleting or sorting shows the wrong value next to each label.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Why is using the array index as a key a problem?
blocks.answer:
The index describes the position, not the item. When the list is filtered, sorted, or an item is inserted at the top, the same index now points to a different item. React keeps the component instance (and its state, DOM, focus, and uncontrolled input values) for that index, so state ends up attached to the wrong data. It also forces unnecessary updates because every item after the change appears to have new props.

Index keys are fine for static, never-reordered lists such as a fixed set of navigation links.
blocks.explanation: Mention concrete symptoms (wrong input values, animation glitches) to show real-world experience.

blocks.title: Component defined inside a component
blocks.question: A `SearchPage` declares `function ResultRow() {...}` inside its body and renders `<ResultRow />` items. Typing in an input inside each row loses focus on every keystroke. Why?
blocks.answer: Each render of `SearchPage` creates a new `ResultRow` function, which React treats as a different component type. Different type at the same position means unmount + remount, so DOM nodes and state (including focus) are recreated.
blocks.explanation:
Move the component declaration to module scope and pass data through props.

[Further reading](https://react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state#different-components-at-the-same-position-reset-state)
hints: How does React compare element types between renders?
Is `ResultRow` the same function each render?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A kanban board with drag-and-drop shows cards briefly flashing old content and losing focus after moves. What do you check?
blocks.answer:
1. Keys: every card must use its persistent id, not the index within the column.
2. Moving between columns changes the parent, so the card remounts; keep per-card UI state that must survive in a store keyed by id, not inside the card component.
3. Ensure no component types are created inline during render (HOCs called inside render, inline component definitions).
4. Make updates immutable so memoised cards that did not move can bail out.
5. For animations, use a stable id for layout animations or React 19.3 `<ViewTransition>` with a `name` per card.
6. Profile a drag to ensure only the affected columns re-render.
blocks.explanation: Connects keys, tree position, and state ownership to a real UI symptom.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Using `Math.random()` or `Date.now()` as keys to silence the warning.
blocks.whyItHappens: It removes the console warning so it seems fixed.
blocks.correctApproach: A new key every render forces every item to remount, destroying state and hurting performance. Use a stable id from the data; generate ids once when the data is created, not during render.

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Treat keys as data identity and design state ownership around it.
keyPoints: Use backend ids or ids generated when the item is created.
Use `key` intentionally to reset a component (e.g. per-user forms).
Keep component declarations at module scope.
Lint with `react/no-array-index-key` and `react/no-unstable-nested-components`.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Keys give list items identity.
- State lives at a tree position + key.
- Different type or key ⇒ remount.
- Index keys only for static lists.

Official references

- https://react.dev/learn/rendering-lists
- https://react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state

title: Events and Forms
description: Synthetic events, delegation at the root, controlled vs uncontrolled inputs, and form libraries with schema validation.

blocks.title: Events in React
blocks.content:
React attaches handlers with camelCase props (`onClick`, `onChange`) and wraps native events in a SyntheticEvent with a consistent cross-browser API. Since React 17 listeners are attached to the root container instead of `document`, which makes multiple React roots and micro-frontends safer.

Handlers are the right place for side effects triggered by the user: submitting, navigating, sending analytics. Pass a function, not the result of calling it: `onClick={handleClick}`, not `onClick={handleClick()}`.

`onChange` in React fires on every keystroke for inputs (like the native `input` event), not on blur.
keyPoints: Handlers run side effects caused by user actions.
React delegates events at the root container.
`e.stopPropagation()` and `e.preventDefault()` work as in the DOM.
React `onChange` ≈ native `input` event.

blocks.title: Controlled vs uncontrolled inputs
blocks.content:
A controlled input's value lives in React state: `value={name}` plus `onChange`. React is the single source of truth, which makes instant validation, formatting, and conditional UI easy, at the cost of a re-render per keystroke.

An uncontrolled input keeps its value in the DOM; you read it on submit through `FormData` or a ref, and set the starting value with `defaultValue`. React 19 form Actions (`<form action={fn}>`) embrace this: the action receives `FormData`, and React resets the form after a successful submission.

Large forms usually use React Hook Form (uncontrolled by default, register via refs) with a Zod schema resolver, giving minimal re-renders and type-safe validation shared with the server.
keyPoints: Controlled: `value` + `onChange`; uncontrolled: `defaultValue` + read on submit.
Switching from undefined to a value triggers the controlled/uncontrolled warning.
React 19 `<form action>` receives `FormData` and supports pending state.
Share validation schemas (Zod) between client and server.

blocks.title: Uncontrolled form with a React 19 Action and validation
blocks.explanation: The form stays uncontrolled; the Action validates `FormData` with the same schema the server can reuse. `useActionState` tracks the result and pending state without manual `useState` flags.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: When would you choose a controlled input over an uncontrolled one?
blocks.answer:
Choose controlled when the UI needs the value on every keystroke: live validation, input masking, enabling/disabling other fields, dependent dropdowns, or syncing with URL/search state.

Choose uncontrolled when you only need the value on submit, for performance in very large forms, for file inputs (always uncontrolled), or when using React 19 form Actions and progressive enhancement with server functions.

In practice, libraries like React Hook Form combine both: uncontrolled registration for speed, with `watch`/`Controller` for the fields that need reactive behaviour.
blocks.explanation: Show you understand the trade-off (re-render per keystroke vs. reactive UI), not a single 'right' answer.

blocks.title: The controlled ↔ uncontrolled warning
blocks.question: `<input value={user.nickname} onChange={...} />` logs 'A component is changing an uncontrolled input to be controlled'. The nickname loads asynchronously. Why?
blocks.answer: On the first render `user.nickname` is `undefined`, so React treats the input as uncontrolled. When the data arrives the value becomes a string, so it switches to controlled. Use `value={user.nickname ?? ''}` or render the form after data loads.
blocks.explanation:
An input must stay in one mode for its lifetime. `undefined` and `null` mean 'no value prop'.

[Further reading](https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/input#controlling-an-input-with-a-state-variable)
hints: What does React consider `value={undefined}`?
What changes when data loads?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: An insurance quote form has 120 fields across 6 steps, and typing lags on low-end devices. How would you architect it?
blocks.answer:
1. Measure: profile a keystroke; typical cause is one top-level `useState` object re-rendering every field.
2. Use React Hook Form (uncontrolled registration) so typing does not re-render the whole form; subscribe narrowly with `useWatch` only where needed.
3. Define one Zod schema per step and compose them; reuse the schema on the server.
4. Persist each step's draft (session storage or server) so refreshes and step navigation do not lose data.
5. Lazy-load heavy widgets (address lookups, date pickers) per step.
6. Make validation accessible: link errors with `aria-describedby`, move focus to the first invalid field on submit, and announce errors.
7. Track field-level drop-off analytics and test the slowest target device.
blocks.explanation: Combines rendering performance, validation architecture, accessibility, and resilience.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Calling the handler during render: `onClick={handleDelete(id)}`.
blocks.whyItHappens: It looks like passing an argument, but the expression is evaluated immediately on every render.
blocks.correctApproach: Pass a function: `onClick={() => handleDelete(id)}`, or bind data via a data attribute and a single handler.

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Pick the form strategy by requirements, and keep validation in one schema.
keyPoints: Default to uncontrolled + Actions for simple forms.
Use React Hook Form + Zod for large or dynamic forms.
Never trust client validation alone — validate again on the server.
Associate labels, errors, and descriptions for accessibility.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- React events are delegated at the root.
- Controlled = state-driven; uncontrolled = DOM-driven.
- React 19 `<form action>` + `useActionState` for submissions.
- Schema validation shared with the server.

Official references

- https://react.dev/learn/responding-to-events
- https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/input
- https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/form
