title: SSR, Streaming, and Hydration
description: Rendering strategies (CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR), streaming with Suspense, selective hydration, and hydration mismatches.

blocks.title: Rendering strategies in simple language
blocks.content:
- **CSR** (client-side rendering): the server sends an almost empty HTML file; JavaScript renders everything. Simple hosting, slower first content, weaker SEO.
- **SSR** (server-side rendering): the server renders HTML per request, then the client **hydrates** it — React attaches event handlers and state to the existing HTML.
- **SSG** (static generation): HTML is rendered at build time.
- **ISR/revalidation**: static pages regenerated periodically or on demand.

Hydration makes server HTML interactive. Until it finishes, users can see content but interactions may not work.
keyPoints: CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR trade freshness, speed, and cost.
Hydration attaches React to server HTML.
Server and client must render the same initial output.
Choose per route, not per app.

blocks.title: Streaming and selective hydration
blocks.content:
React's streaming APIs (`renderToPipeableStream`, `renderToReadableStream`) send HTML in chunks. Content inside Suspense boundaries can stream later, so the shell arrives fast.

On the client, `hydrateRoot` hydrates **selectively**: each Suspense boundary hydrates independently, and React prioritises boundaries the user interacts with. Slow widgets no longer block interactivity of the rest of the page.

React 19.2 added Partial Pre-rendering APIs (`prerender` + `resume`) to pre-render a static shell and resume dynamic parts at request time.
keyPoints: Streaming sends the shell first.
Suspense boundaries = streaming + hydration units.
Interaction-driven hydration priority.
Partial pre-rendering combines static shells with dynamic holes.

blocks.title: Avoiding a hydration mismatch with dates
blocks.explanation: Initial output is identical on both sides; the localised value is applied after hydration. Alternatives: render with the user's timezone known on the server, or use `suppressHydrationWarning` on that single text node.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What causes hydration mismatches, and why do they matter?
blocks.answer:
A mismatch happens when the client's first render differs from the server HTML. Common causes: `Date.now()`/`Math.random()` during render, timezone or locale differences, reading `window`/`localStorage` during render, browser extensions mutating the DOM, invalid HTML nesting (`
` inside `

`), and data that changed between server render and client hydration. They matter because React must patch or re-render content on the client, which costs performance and can cause visible flicker or lost event bindings. React 19 reports mismatches with a single diff-style error.
blocks.explanation: Concrete causes + consequences.

blocks.title: typeof window checks during render
blocks.question: A component renders `{typeof window !== 'undefined' ? <MobileNav /> : <DesktopNav />}`. Hydration warns and the nav flickers. Why?
blocks.answer: On the server `window` is undefined (DesktopNav), but on the client's hydration render it exists (MobileNav), so the first client render differs from the server HTML. Render the same output first, then switch after mount (effect/`useSyncExternalStore` with a server snapshot), or use CSS media queries.
blocks.explanation:
The first client render must match the server render.

[Further reading](https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/client/hydrateRoot#handling-different-client-and-server-content)
hints: What does each environment render initially?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: Your e-commerce site is CSR-only; SEO and LCP are poor. Leadership asks for SSR. How do you approach it?
blocks.answer:
1. Choose a framework (Next.js or React Router framework mode) rather than hand-rolled SSR.
2. Classify routes: marketing/product pages → SSG/ISR or SSR with caching; account/checkout → SSR or CSR behind auth.
3. Audit browser-only code (window, localStorage, third-party widgets) and isolate it in client-only components.
4. Introduce streaming with Suspense around slow sections (reviews, recommendations).
5. Cache at the CDN with appropriate revalidation; monitor TTFB to ensure SSR doesn't make it worse.
6. Migrate route by route behind traffic splitting; track LCP, conversion, and error rates.
blocks.explanation: Route-level strategy, browser-code isolation, and measured rollout.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Assuming SSR automatically makes the app fast.
blocks.whyItHappens: SSR improves first paint, so it's seen as a universal fix.
blocks.correctApproach: SSR can hurt TTFB and still ship large JS. Combine with streaming, caching, and reducing client JavaScript (Server Components).

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Pick rendering per route and protect hydration.
keyPoints: Same initial render on server and client.
Stream slow content behind Suspense.
Isolate browser-only code.
Measure TTFB, LCP, and INP together.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR per route.
- Hydration attaches React to server HTML.
- Streaming + selective hydration via Suspense.
- Avoid non-deterministic first renders.

Official references

- https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/server
- https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/client/hydrateRoot
- https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/static

title: React Server Components
description: Server vs Client Components, the 'use client' boundary, serialisable props, composition patterns, and bundle impact.

blocks.title: Server Components in simple language
blocks.content:
React Server Components (RSC) run only on the server (at build time or per request). They can be `async`, read databases or files directly, and their code is **never sent to the browser**. They render to a special serialised format that the client merges into the UI.

Client Components are the familiar components with state, effects, and event handlers. You mark the entry point of client code with `'use client'` at the top of a file; everything that file imports becomes part of the client bundle.

In frameworks such as Next.js App Router, components are Server Components by default.
keyPoints: Server Components: no state/effects, zero client JS.
`'use client'` marks a module boundary into the client bundle.
Server Components can be async and access backend resources.
Default in RSC frameworks.

blocks.title: Boundaries, serialisation, and composition
blocks.content:
Props passed from Server to Client Components must be serialisable: primitives, plain objects/arrays, Dates, Maps/Sets, promises, JSX, and Server Functions — but not regular functions or class instances.

A Client Component can't import a Server Component, but it can **receive** one as `children` or another prop. This 'donut' pattern keeps interactive shells small: `<ClientTabs>{<ServerReport />}</ClientTabs>`.

Push `'use client'` as low as possible (leaf interactive components) to minimise JavaScript. React 19.3 also allows Server Components to render a Context provider imported from a client module directly.
keyPoints: Only serialisable props cross the boundary.
Pass Server Components as children to Client Components.
Keep `'use client'` at the leaves.
Use `server-only` to prevent server code leaking into client bundles.

blocks.title: Server data + small client island
blocks.explanation: The database code and row rendering stay on the server. Only the small filter input ships JavaScript. A DTO prevents leaking internal fields to the client.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: How do Server Components differ from SSR?
blocks.answer:
SSR renders Client Components to HTML on the server, then ships **all** their JavaScript to hydrate them. Server Components never hydrate and ship **no** JavaScript; their output is serialised and merged into the tree, and they can be re-fetched without losing client state.

They're complementary: an RSC framework server-renders the Server Component output and the Client Components to HTML for the first load (SSR), then hydrates only the Client Components.
blocks.explanation: The bundle-size and hydration difference is the key.

blocks.title: Passing a function to a Client Component
blocks.question: A Server Component renders `<DeleteButton onDelete={() => db.delete(id)} />` where DeleteButton is a Client Component. It fails with 'Functions cannot be passed directly to Client Components'. Why, and how do you fix it?
blocks.answer: Props crossing the server→client boundary must be serialisable, and ordinary closures aren't. Define a Server Function (`'use server'`) for the delete and pass that (or import it in the client component); React serialises a reference the client can call.
blocks.explanation:
Server Functions are the only functions that can cross the boundary.

[Further reading](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-client#serializable-types)
hints: What can be serialised across the boundary?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A Next.js App Router project marked the root layout with 'use client' 'to make things work', and the JS bundle doubled. How do you fix the architecture?
blocks.answer:
1. Find why: usually a context provider or hook in the layout. Extract providers into a small `Providers` client component and render it inside a server layout.
2. Push `'use client'` down to interactive leaves; convert data-display components back to Server Components.
3. Use the children/donut pattern for client wrappers (modals, tabs) that contain server content.
4. Add `import 'server-only'` to data-access modules to prevent accidental client imports.
5. Analyse bundles before/after and set a budget in CI.
6. Educate the team with a short boundary guideline and lint rules.
blocks.explanation: Typical real-world RSC mistake and its systematic fix.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Sending full database records (including internal fields) as props to Client Components.
blocks.whyItHappens: Props feel internal, but they're serialised into the page payload.
blocks.correctApproach: Map data to DTOs with only the fields the client needs; consider React's taint APIs or framework guards for sensitive values.

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Default to server, opt into client for interactivity.
keyPoints: Keep client islands small and at the leaves.
Use DTOs; never leak secrets via props.
Fetch data in Server Components close to the source.
Measure client JS per route.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- RSC run on the server; no client JS.
- `'use client'` marks client module boundaries.
- Serialisable props only; Server Functions for actions.
- Compose servers inside clients via children.

Official references

- https://react.dev/reference/rsc/server-components
- https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-client
- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components

title: Server Functions ('use server')
description: Defining Server Functions, calling them from forms and Client Components, security, validation, and revalidation.

blocks.title: Server Functions in simple language
blocks.content:
A Server Function is an async function marked with `'use server'` that runs on the server but can be called from the client. The framework creates an HTTP endpoint and passes a reference to the client; calling it sends the arguments over the network.

When used as a form `action` (or via `useActionState`), they're often called Server Actions. Forms can submit even before JavaScript loads, which gives progressive enhancement.

`'use server'` marks functions callable from the client — it is **not** how you mark Server Components (those need no directive).
keyPoints: `'use server'` = client-callable server function.
Arguments and return values must be serialisable.
Works with forms, `useActionState`, and transitions.
Progressive enhancement for forms.

blocks.title: Security model
blocks.content:
Every Server Function is effectively a **public API endpoint**. Anyone can call it with any arguments, not only your UI. Therefore:

- Authenticate and authorise inside the function on every call.
- Validate all arguments with a schema.
- Don't trust IDs from the client — check ownership.
- Rate-limit sensitive operations.
- Return minimal data; avoid leaking errors.

After mutating, revalidate cached data (e.g. `revalidatePath`/`updateTag` in Next.js) so the UI reflects the change.
keyPoints: Treat as public endpoints.
Auth + authorisation + validation every call.
Return minimal, typed results.
Revalidate caches after mutations.

blocks.title: Secure Server Function with validation
blocks.explanation: Authentication, schema validation, and ownership checks happen inside the function because it can be invoked directly over HTTP.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Are Server Functions safe because they aren't visible in client code?
blocks.answer: No. Their implementation stays on the server, but they're exposed as network endpoints with stable identifiers, and any user (or script) can call them with arbitrary arguments. Hidden code is not access control. Each function must perform authentication, authorisation, input validation, and rate limiting as you would for a REST endpoint.
blocks.explanation: Security mindset is the main evaluation point.

blocks.title: Inline Server Function capturing variables
blocks.question: A Server Component defines an inline `'use server'` function that closes over a variable `userId` from the component. Is `userId` trustworthy when the function runs?
blocks.answer: Captured values are serialised and sent to the client (encrypted by frameworks like Next.js), then sent back on invocation. You still shouldn't rely on them for authorisation — re-derive the user from the session on the server inside the function.
blocks.explanation:
Frameworks encrypt closures, but defence in depth requires server-side checks and avoiding sensitive captures.

[Further reading](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/server-functions)
hints: Where do captured closure values travel?
Where should identity come from?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A security review found that a 'deleteComment' Server Action deletes any comment by id. How do you remediate and prevent recurrence?
blocks.answer:
1. Hotfix: add session auth and ownership/role checks; deploy immediately.
2. Audit all Server Functions for auth, validation, and ownership checks.
3. Introduce a wrapper (`createSafeAction(schema, authorize, handler)`) that enforces validation and authorisation by construction.
4. Add tests that call actions directly with other users' ids.
5. Add rate limiting and audit logging for destructive actions.
6. Update guidelines/code review checklists; add lint rules flagging unwrapped `'use server'` exports.
blocks.explanation: Remediation + systemic prevention.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Using `'use server'` at the top of a file to make its components 'server components'.
blocks.whyItHappens: The directive names look symmetrical with `'use client'`.
blocks.correctApproach: Server Components need no directive. `'use server'` exports become client-callable endpoints — only put server functions there.

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Build Server Functions like public APIs.
keyPoints: Validate and authorise every call.
Wrap actions in a shared safe helper.
Revalidate the right cache entries.
Combine with `useActionState`/`useOptimistic` for UX.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- `'use server'` exposes server functions to the client.
- Serialisable args/returns.
- Public endpoint security model.
- Revalidate after mutations.

Official references

- https://react.dev/reference/rsc/server-functions
- https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-server
- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/updating-data

title: Next.js App Router Architecture
description: Layouts, loading and error files, caching and revalidation, route handlers, middleware/proxy, and deployment considerations.

blocks.title: App Router in simple language
blocks.content:
Next.js App Router is the most widely used React Server Components framework. Routes are folders under `app/`; special files define behaviour:

- `layout.tsx` — shared UI that persists across navigations.
- `page.tsx` — the route's UI.
- `loading.tsx` — an automatic Suspense fallback.
- `error.tsx` — a route-level error boundary (a Client Component).
- `route.ts` — API route handlers.

Server Components are the default; data is fetched directly in components with `async/await`.
keyPoints: File-system routing with special files.
Layouts persist and don't re-render on navigation.
`loading`/`error` map to Suspense/Error Boundaries.
Server Components by default.

blocks.title: Caching and rendering
blocks.content:
Recent Next.js versions make caching explicit: dynamic rendering by default, with opt-in caching via the `'use cache'` directive and `cacheLife`/`cacheTag`, plus Partial Prerendering that combines a static shell with dynamic streamed parts. Mutations call `revalidateTag`/`updateTag`/`revalidatePath` to refresh cached data.

Request-time APIs (`cookies()`, `headers()`, `searchParams`) make a segment dynamic. Understand which parts of a page are static, cached, or per-request — most production bugs are 'stale data' or 'unexpectedly dynamic' issues.

Check the exact caching APIs for your Next.js version; they have changed across major releases.
keyPoints: Know which segments are static, cached, or dynamic.
Tag cached data and invalidate after mutations.
Request-time APIs make segments dynamic.
Caching APIs vary by version — verify in docs.

blocks.title: Route segment with loading, error, and cached data
blocks.explanation: Product data is cached and tagged for targeted invalidation; live stock streams per request inside Suspense.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What's the difference between a layout and a template in the App Router?
blocks.answer: A `layout` persists across navigations between its child routes — its state is preserved and it doesn't remount. A `template` re-mounts on every navigation, creating fresh state and re-running effects, which is useful for per-page animations or resetting forms. Use layouts by default.
blocks.explanation: Practical framework knowledge.

blocks.title: Why did my static page become dynamic?
blocks.question: A product page that should be static is rendered on every request after someone added a personalised greeting that calls `cookies()` in the page. Why?
blocks.answer: Reading request-time data (`cookies()`, `headers()`, `searchParams`) opts that segment into dynamic rendering. Move the personalised part into a small component wrapped in Suspense (so the shell can stay static/pre-rendered) or fetch it on the client.
blocks.explanation:
Isolate request-specific data to keep the rest of the page cacheable.

[Further reading](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/partial-prerendering)
hints: Which APIs depend on the incoming request?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: After a CMS update, editors see changes only after hours, but checkout pages show stale prices too. How do you design caching for the site?
blocks.answer:
1. Classify data by freshness: CMS content (minutes, event-driven), product catalog (event-driven), prices and stock (real-time), user data (per request).
2. Tag cached fetches (`product:id`, `cms:page:slug`) and trigger `revalidateTag` from CMS/product webhooks.
3. Never cache prices/stock at page level; stream them dynamically inside Suspense.
4. Make checkout fully dynamic and authoritative on the server.
5. Document caching rules per route and add tests or monitoring that detect stale data (e.g. compare rendered price with API).
blocks.explanation: Data-classification-driven caching design.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Making the whole page dynamic because one component needs request data.
blocks.whyItHappens: It's the quickest way to remove a stale-data bug.
blocks.correctApproach: Isolate dynamic parts behind Suspense and keep the shell static or cached.

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Make rendering and caching decisions explicit per segment.
keyPoints: Use `loading`/`error` files for every major segment.
Tag cached data; invalidate from webhooks and mutations.
Keep request-time APIs in small leaves.
Check build output to confirm static vs dynamic.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- App Router = RSC framework with file-based routing.
- `layout`, `page`, `loading`, `error`, `route`.
- Explicit caching with tags and revalidation.
- Request APIs make segments dynamic.

Official references

- https://nextjs.org/docs/app
- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/caching-and-revalidating
- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/partial-prerendering

title: Testing Components with React Testing Library
description: Testing behaviour not implementation, query priorities, user-event, testing hooks, and the testing pyramid for React.

blocks.title: Testing philosophy in simple language
blocks.content:
React Testing Library (RTL) encourages tests that resemble how users use your app: find elements by role and label, interact with them, and assert on what the user sees. Avoid testing implementation details like internal state, private methods, or component instance structure — those tests break during refactors even when behaviour is unchanged.

Typical stack in 2026: Vitest (or Jest) + jsdom/happy-dom + RTL + `@testing-library/user-event`, with Playwright for end-to-end and component tests in a real browser.
keyPoints: Test behaviour, not implementation.
Query like a user (roles, labels, text).
Use `user-event` for realistic interactions.
Combine unit, integration, and E2E tests.

blocks.title: Query priority and async assertions
blocks.content:
Query priority: `getByRole` (with `name`) → `getByLabelText` → `getByPlaceholderText` → `getByText` → `getByDisplayValue` → `getByAltText`/`getByTitle` → `getByTestId` as a last resort.

- `getBy*` throws if not found (synchronous presence).
- `queryBy*` returns null (assert absence).
- `findBy*` returns a promise and waits (async appearance).

`user-event` methods are async: always `await user.click(...)`. Prefer `findBy` over `waitFor` + `getBy` for appearing elements.
keyPoints: Prefer `getByRole(..., { name })`.
`queryBy` for absence, `findBy` for async.
`await` every user-event call.
Role queries double as accessibility checks.

blocks.title: Behaviour-focused test with user-event
blocks.explanation: The component test only uses what a user can see and do; the hook test uses `renderHook` and `act` for state updates outside events.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Why does React Testing Library discourage testing implementation details?
blocks.answer: Tests coupled to internals (state variable names, component structure, calling instance methods) fail when you refactor without changing behaviour — false negatives — and can pass while the user-facing behaviour is broken — false positives. Testing through the UI the way users interact gives confidence that the feature works and lets you refactor freely (e.g. switch `useState` to `useReducer`, or adopt the React Compiler) without rewriting tests.
blocks.explanation: Mention refactoring safety.

blocks.title: Asserting that something is gone
blocks.question: A test does `expect(screen.getByText('Loading…')).not.toBeInTheDocument()` and fails with 'Unable to find an element'. Why?
blocks.answer: `getBy*` throws immediately when the element isn't found, before the assertion runs. Use `queryByText` for absence, or `await waitForElementToBeRemoved(() => screen.queryByText('Loading…'))` for something that disappears asynchronously.
blocks.explanation:
Choose the query variant that matches the expectation: get (present), query (maybe absent), find (eventually present).

[Further reading](https://testing-library.com/docs/queries/about/#types-of-queries)
hints: What does `getBy` do when nothing matches?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: The React app has 85% coverage but production bugs keep slipping through, and tests break on every refactor. How do you improve the testing strategy?
blocks.answer:
1. Analyse escaped bugs: which layer would have caught them (integration flows, API contracts, browser behaviour)?
2. Replace snapshot-heavy and implementation-detail tests with behaviour tests using RTL queries by role.
3. Add integration tests for key flows with MSW-mocked APIs instead of mocking modules/hooks.
4. Add a small set of Playwright E2E tests for critical journeys (login, checkout) and component tests for complex widgets in real browsers.
5. Track meaningful metrics (escaped defects, flaky test rate) rather than coverage alone.
6. Lint with `eslint-plugin-testing-library` to enforce good patterns.
blocks.explanation: Strategy driven by escaped defects, not coverage numbers.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Using `container.querySelector('.btn-primary')` or test ids for everything.
blocks.whyItHappens: It's familiar from DOM scripting and quick to write.
blocks.correctApproach: Query by accessible role and name. This also surfaces accessibility gaps (unlabelled buttons).

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Write tests users would recognise.
keyPoints: Role/label queries first.
`userEvent.setup()` and `await` interactions.
Mock the network, not your own modules.
Keep a thin E2E layer for critical journeys.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Test behaviour through the UI.
- Query priority: role → label → text → test id.
- `get`/`query`/`find` semantics.
- `renderHook` for hooks.

Official references

- https://testing-library.com/docs/react-testing-library/intro/
- https://testing-library.com/docs/queries/about/#priority
- https://testing-library.com/docs/user-event/intro

title: Testing Async UI and APIs with MSW
description: Mock Service Worker for network mocking, testing loading/error states, act warnings, fake timers, and flaky tests.

blocks.title: Mocking the network, not the code
blocks.content:
Mock Service Worker (MSW) intercepts requests at the network level — in Node for tests and in the browser for development. Your components and data libraries run their real code paths (fetch, TanStack Query, retries), and only the server response is faked.

Define default happy-path handlers, then override per test with `server.use(...)` for errors, empty states, and slow responses. Reset handlers after each test.
keyPoints: MSW intercepts at the network layer.
Same handlers for tests, Storybook, and local dev.
Override per test for edge cases.
Reset handlers between tests.

blocks.title: act, async utilities, and flakiness
blocks.content:
React must finish processing updates before you assert. RTL wraps renders and user-event interactions in `act` for you; warnings about 'not wrapped in act(...)' usually mean an async update happened after the test finished or wasn't awaited — wait for the final UI with `findBy*`.

For timers (debounce, polling) use fake timers and advance them, and configure `userEvent.setup({ advanceTimers: vi.advanceTimersByTime })`.

Flaky tests often come from shared state between tests (query cache, MSW handlers, localStorage). Create a fresh `QueryClient` with `retry: false` per test.
keyPoints: Await the final state with `findBy`.
`act` warnings = unawaited async updates.
Fake timers for debounce/polling.
Isolate caches and storage per test.

blocks.title: Testing loading, success, and error with MSW
blocks.explanation: Each test gets a fresh cache, unhandled requests fail loudly, and error states are tested by overriding one handler.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Why prefer MSW over mocking fetch or your API module with vi.mock?
blocks.answer: Module mocks bypass real code: serialisation, headers, error parsing, retries, and caching logic aren't exercised, and mocks drift from the real API shape. MSW keeps the whole client stack real and only fakes the HTTP boundary, so tests catch more bugs. Handlers can be shared with Storybook and local development, and generated from OpenAPI specs to stay aligned with the backend.
blocks.explanation: Emphasise fidelity and reuse.

blocks.title: act() warning after the test passes
blocks.question: A test asserts the initial render and passes, but logs 'An update to Profile inside a test was not wrapped in act(...)'. Why?
blocks.answer: The component started an async request; its response resolved after the assertion and updated state outside any awaited test step. Await the final UI (`await screen.findBy...`) so the update happens within the test, or mock the request to resolve before asserting.
blocks.explanation:
The warning signals that the test isn't observing all of the component's behaviour.

[Further reading](https://testing-library.com/docs/dom-testing-library/api-async/)
hints: What happened after the last assertion?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: CI has a 7% flaky failure rate in the React test suite. How do you systematically fix it?
blocks.answer:
1. Collect data: rerun failing tests, tag flaky ones, and group by root cause.
2. Fix shared state: fresh QueryClient/store per test, reset MSW handlers, clear storage, restore mocks.
3. Replace arbitrary waits with `findBy`/`waitFor` on specific UI.
4. Control time and randomness: fake timers, seeded data, fixed timezone/locale in the test environment.
5. Fail on unhandled requests and console errors to surface hidden problems.
6. Quarantine with an owner and deadline rather than adding retries permanently; track flake rate as a team metric.
blocks.explanation: Root-cause categories + process.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Using `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 500))` to wait for UI.
blocks.whyItHappens: It works locally and seems simple.
blocks.correctApproach: Wait for a specific condition with `findBy*`/`waitFor`. Arbitrary sleeps are slow and flaky on CI.

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Make async tests deterministic.
keyPoints: MSW with `onUnhandledRequest: 'error'`.
Fresh caches per test; retries off.
Fake timers for time-based logic.
Treat flaky tests as bugs.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- MSW mocks HTTP, keeps code real.
- Await final UI with `findBy`.
- act warnings = unobserved updates.
- Isolate state to avoid flakiness.

Official references

- https://mswjs.io/docs/
- https://testing-library.com/docs/dom-testing-library/api-async/
- https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/guides/testing

title: TypeScript Patterns for React
description: Typing props and children, events, refs, generic components, discriminated unions, polymorphic components, and ComponentProps.

blocks.title: Typing components in simple language
blocks.content:
Type props with an interface or type alias and destructure them in the function signature. Prefer plain function components over `React.FC` (which historically added implicit `children`).

Useful built-in types: `ReactNode` (anything renderable), `ComponentProps<'button'>`/`ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'>` (native props), `Ref<T>` (refs as props in React 19), `ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>`, `FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>`, and `Dispatch<SetStateAction<T>>`.

Let TypeScript infer hook types where possible (`useState(0)`), and annotate when the initial value doesn't describe all states (`useState<User | null>(null)`).
keyPoints: Type props explicitly; avoid `React.FC`.
Extend native props with `ComponentProps<'el'>`.
`ReactNode` for children.
Annotate `useState` for unions/null.

blocks.title: Advanced patterns
blocks.content:
**Discriminated unions** model mutually exclusive props: a `Button` is either a link (`href`) or a button (`onClick`), never both.

**Generic components** keep type information flowing: `<Select<T> options={T[]} getLabel={(o: T) => string} onChange={(o: T) => void} />`.

**Polymorphic components** (`as` prop) need careful typing so allowed props change with the element; many design systems use an `asChild`/Slot pattern instead to keep types simpler.

Generate API types from OpenAPI/GraphQL schemas, and validate at runtime with Zod — TypeScript types disappear at runtime.
keyPoints: Unions make invalid prop combos impossible.
Generics preserve item types through callbacks.
Prefer Slot/`asChild` over complex polymorphism.
Runtime validation for external data.

blocks.title: Generic, accessible Select component
blocks.explanation: The generic `T` flows from `options` into `onChange`, so consumers get typed objects back instead of strings. `useId` links the label for accessibility.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: How would you type a component that renders either a link or a button?
blocks.answer:
Use a discriminated union so the props are mutually exclusive (see the code above): one branch requires `href` and accepts anchor props, the other forbids `href` and accepts button props.

Inside, narrow with `if (props.href !== undefined)` and render `<a>` or `<button>`. Consumers can't pass `onClick`-only button props alongside `href` incorrectly, and native attributes are typed for each element.
blocks.explanation: Union-based narrowing shows TypeScript depth.

blocks.title: useState([]) typed as never[]
blocks.question: `const [items, setItems] = useState([]);` then `setItems([{ id: '1' }])` fails to compile with 'not assignable to never'. Why?
blocks.answer: TypeScript infers the state type from the initial value; an empty array literal is inferred as `never[]`. Provide the type argument: `useState<Item[]>([])`.
blocks.explanation:
Annotate when the initial value doesn't represent all future values.

[Further reading](https://react.dev/learn/typescript#typing-usestate)
hints: What type does TypeScript infer for `[]`?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: Your design system's types are so complex (deep polymorphism) that editor autocomplete is slow and errors are unreadable. What do you do?
blocks.answer:
1. Measure type-check performance (`tsc --extendedDiagnostics`, trace) to find hot types.
2. Replace generic `as`-polymorphism with the `asChild`/Slot pattern or a few explicit variants.
3. Prefer interfaces and named types over huge intersections; avoid deeply recursive conditional types.
4. Export simple, documented prop types (`ButtonProps`) for consumers.
5. Add type tests (`expectTypeOf`, `tsd`) to lock the public API.
6. Re-measure editor responsiveness and build times.
blocks.explanation: Pragmatic type design over cleverness.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Using `any` for event handlers or API responses to silence errors.
blocks.whyItHappens: It unblocks quickly when types are unfamiliar.
blocks.correctApproach: Use the specific React event types and validate external data with schemas that infer types (`z.infer`).

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Let types encode your component contracts.
keyPoints: Unions for exclusive variants.
Extend native element props.
Generics for data-driven components.
Runtime validation at system boundaries.

blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Type props; avoid `React.FC`.
- `ComponentProps`, `ReactNode`, event types.
- Unions and generics for safe APIs.
- Runtime validation for external data.

Official references

title: Accessibility in React Apps
description: Semantic HTML, ARIA, focus management on route changes and dialogs, useId, live regions, and automated a11y testing.

blocks.title: Accessibility in simple language
blocks.content:
Accessible React apps start with semantic HTML: real `<button>`s, `<a href>`s, `<label>`s, headings, and landmarks. Native elements give keyboard support and screen-reader semantics for free.

React-specific concerns: client-side routing doesn't move focus or announce page changes like a full page load does; dynamic content updates need live regions; and generated ids must be stable across server and client — use `useId()`.

ARIA is a supplement, not a replacement: 'No ARIA is better than bad ARIA'.
keyPoints: Semantic elements first.
Manage focus on route changes and dialogs.
`useId` for label/description associations.
ARIA only when HTML can't express it.

blocks.title: Focus, announcements, and testing
blocks.content:
On navigation, move focus to the main heading or a skip target and update the document title. For dialogs, trap focus inside, restore it on close, and close on Escape — the native `<dialog>` element helps.

Announce async results (form errors, 'saved', search counts) with `role="status"` or `role="alert"` regions.

Test with keyboard only, a screen reader (VoiceOver, NVDA), automated tools (axe via `vitest-axe`/`jest-axe`, Playwright axe), and lint with `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y`. Target WCAG 2.2 AA.
keyPoints: Focus to content on route change.
Dialogs: trap, restore, Escape.
Live regions for async feedback.
Automated + manual testing.

blocks.title: Accessible form field with useId and error announcement
blocks.explanation: `useId` produces ids that match between server and client. The input is linked to its description and error, and the error is announced when it appears.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Why use useId instead of generating ids with a counter or Math.random?
blocks.answer: `useId` generates ids that are unique per component instance and **identical on the server and client**, preventing hydration mismatches. Module-level counters differ between server and client render order, and `Math.random` differs every render. `useId` is meant for accessibility attributes (`htmlFor`, `aria-describedby`), not for list keys.
blocks.explanation: Tie to SSR consistency.

blocks.title: Clickable div
blocks.question: A card uses `<div onClick={open}>` and works with a mouse. What accessibility problems does it have?
blocks.answer: It isn't focusable, has no role, and doesn't respond to Enter/Space, so keyboard and screen-reader users can't use it. Use a `<button>` (or an `<a href>` for navigation), or add role, tabIndex, and key handlers — the native element is far simpler.
blocks.explanation:
Native interactive elements provide focus, keyboard behaviour, and semantics automatically.

[Further reading](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Roles/button_role)
hints: Can a keyboard user reach and activate it?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A legal audit flagged your React SPA for WCAG violations across 60 screens. How do you lead remediation?
blocks.answer:
1. Triage: run automated scans across routes, combine with manual audit findings, and prioritise by severity and user impact (blockers first: keyboard traps, unlabelled controls, missing focus management).
2. Fix at the source: shared design-system components (Button, Dialog, Field, Menu) — one fix resolves many screens.
3. Add global fixes: route-change focus and title updates, skip links, landmarks.
4. Add guardrails: jsx-a11y lint, axe in unit and E2E tests, a11y acceptance criteria in tickets.
5. Train the team and include people with disabilities in usability testing.
6. Publish an accessibility statement and track progress to WCAG 2.2 AA.
blocks.explanation: Systemic remediation via design system + guardrails.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Adding `role="button"` and `aria-label` to divs instead of using native elements.
blocks.whyItHappens: It seems like adding ARIA makes anything accessible.
blocks.correctApproach: Use native elements. ARIA changes semantics but doesn't add keyboard behaviour.

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Build accessibility into components and process.
keyPoints: Accessible primitives in the design system.
Focus management for routes and overlays.
Automated axe checks in CI.
Manual screen-reader passes for key flows.
